newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Police nets scarecrow in HK sea hunt for children.
newsitem.headline: Police nets scarecrow in HK sea hunt for children.

text.p: Hong Kong police, who launched a rescue mission in nearby waters for mainland Chinese children feared to have been thrown overboard a smuggling speedboat, have found a scarecrow, police said on Saturday.
The search was launched after police onboard a patrol craft, giving chase to a speedboat trying to sneak into the territory late on Friday, saw two objects being shoved into the sea.
Policemen aboard the patrol craft had believed the objects were children, saying they saw two men and four or five children on the unlit speedboat during the night chase.
A massive rescue mission involving five police launchers and one helicopter was launched immediately in waters around the incident, off the Ninepin islands southeast of Hong Kong.
But what they netted by late Saturday turned out quite unexpected.
"We have scooped up one scarecrow near Ninepins," a marine police source told Reuters.
"This scarecrow might have been dumped by the smugglers. It was very dark last night and we thought they might have thrown children into the sea, but today we have found a scarecrow."
The unexpected find, however, has not dampened resolve - nor the search.
"But we can't really determine if they (the adults) have not dumped out children," the source said.
"As of 7 p.m. (1100 GMT) we have suspended the search because of nightfall, but we will continue tomorrow," he said, adding that two launchers will be used on Sunday.

A growing number of illegal Chinese immigrants, including children, have been caught along border areas in recent weeks after rumours began spreading in southern China that amnesty would be given to illegal migrant children.
But the Hong Kong government has repeatedly stressed that everybody, including children, would be sent back.
An influx of illegal immigrants from China is a major concern in the territory, which reverts to Chinese rule at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
